title: The Fall of Rome (and Why It Didn't Really Fall)

cards.h: The last emperor was a teenager named after Rome's first king and first emperor
cards.b:
In 476 CE, the last western Roman emperor was a boy called Romulus Augustulus. That name mixes Romulus, the legendary founder, and Augustus, the first emperor. 'Augustulus' means 'little Augustus'.

He was deposed, retired to a comfortable villa, and nobody much noticed. So did Rome fall that day?
In the 3rd century CE, civil wars, plagues and invasions nearly broke the empire. Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople in 330 CE. After 395 CE, the empire was usually ruled in two halves.

cards.h: The Huns push, the Goths cross
cards.b:
The Huns, horse-riders from Central Asia, drove Goths into Roman land in 376 CE. In 378, at Adrianople, the Goths killed Emperor Valens and destroyed a Roman army.

Barbarians were not new. Rome had hired them for years. But now whole peoples were settling inside the borders.

In 410 CE the Visigoth king Alaric entered Rome and plundered it for three days. It was the first time in about 800 years that the city had fallen to an enemy. The shock rang across the world.

In 455 the Vandals sacked it again. By then, the western emperors were often puppets of generals.

In 476, a general called Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and sent the royal regalia to the eastern emperor in Constantinople. He ruled Italy as a king.

The Eastern Roman Empire (later called Byzantine) carried on for almost 1,000 more years, until 1453.

Edward Gibbon (The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, 1776-89) blamed barbarians and also Christianity, which he said sapped the old Roman spirit.

Modern historians often look at wars, taxes, plague, climate and politics together. There is no single answer.

Peter Brown and others call this period late antiquity, a time of change more than collapse. Roman law, Latin and the Church survived under new kings.

Others disagree. Bryan Ward-Perkins argued in 2005 that it was a catastrophe: trade shrank, pottery got worse, cities shrank. Archaeology supports him in places like Britain.

The same horsemen hit the Guptas

While Attila's Huns pressed on Rome, other steppe warriors, the Hunas, pressed on the Gupta empire. Skandagupta drove back a first wave around 455 CE, as his Bhitari pillar inscription records.

The Guptas never fully recovered. Toramana broke into Malwa, and his son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala (Sialkot), remembered as a tyrant. Around 528 CE, Yashodharman of Malwa and a Gupta king Baladitya checked him. His fall ended the worst of the raids, but the empire had lost its north-west and its old strength.

Historians are not sure these Huns were related to Attila's. But in both east and west, nomad pressure helped end old orders.

Five things to remember

  1. Rome's troubles were centuries long.
  2. Alaric sacked Rome in 410 CE.
  3. 476 CE ended the Western line.
  4. The East lasted until 1453.
  5. Historians argue between 'fall' and 'transformation'.

Think about it

  • Did a society really end, or just change its rulers?
  • What lessons might this hold for modern states?
